analysis.one_liner: Lets business associations sell group health plans exempt from most state coverage and pricing rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate opened debate on the bill 96-2 in May 2006, but a later vote to end debate and hold a final vote got only 55 of the 60 needed, with 41 of 44 Democrats opposed; the bill never got a final vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let trade associations, chambers of commerce, professional groups, and franchise companies sponsor federally certified 'small business health plans' that only have to be licensed in one state and can operate nationwide. It would also let insurers sell plans in any state whose rules don't match new federal model rating rules and a federal list of standard benefits, voiding state laws on benefits, pricing, and patient protections for those insurers. States that didn't adopt the federal standards would be barred from stopping or penalizing insurers selling under them, and insurers could sue states for damages and legal fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Small business owners and self-employed people could band together through trade associations and chambers of commerce to buy group coverage, potentially at lower premiums. Health insurers and business associations gain the most structurally: insurers could sell skimpier plans free of most state benefit mandates and rating limits across many states, and associations gain a new line of business as plan sponsors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small firms, insurers, and trade associations

how_it_helps.text: Creates federally certified small business health plans sponsored by trade, industry, professional, and chamber of commerce associations, allowing small employers to pool for coverage [S2][S3].
An SBHP only needs to be licensed in its sponsor's home state and can offer coverage in other states without full licensure, preempting state laws on licensure, rating, and benefits [S3].

Requires federal model rating rules for the small-group market and a State Benefit Compendium of harmonized benefit mandates, and voids state rating and benefit laws in any state that does not adopt the federal standards in their entirety [S2][S3].
Bars contribution rates from varying based on health status or industry, and bars plans from excluding employees from coverage based on health status [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People in the small-group and individual insurance markets in states that don't adopt the federal standards would lose state-mandated benefits, external appeals rights, prompt-pay rules, and limits on premium variation. Sicker enrollees would likely pay more as healthier groups migrate into plans exempt from those protections, and state insurance regulators lose their ability to enforce their own rules against the participating insurers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients losing state protections; state regulators

drawbacks.text: In non-adopting states, the bill voids state laws on benefit mandates, rating, and patient protections (including internal and external appeals, direct provider access, and prompt payment of claims) for insurers selling under the federal standards [S4].

Insurers get a federal cause of action for damages, plus attorney's fees, against states that try to apply their own rules, and federal courts get exclusive jurisdiction over disputes under the act [S3][S4].

An SBHP is automatically deemed certified if the Labor Secretary fails to act on its application within 90 days, and the plan itself, not a state, has sole discretion to choose which benefits are covered [S3].

If healthier small employers move into plans exempt from state rating limits and benefit mandates, the remaining state-regulated pool becomes sicker and more expensive, raising premiums for people who stay in it — a risk honest supporters of association plans have long acknowledged (this is general knowledge about adverse selection, not from the sources).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Pooling through associations could genuinely lower premiums for some small firms, and the bill does prohibit health-status discrimination within the plans. But the core mechanism is stripping state insurance rules from any insurer willing to file under the federal standards, in any state that doesn't adopt them wholesale — replacing a patchwork of state consumer protections with a lower federal floor. The savings for some small firms would come largely from thinner benefit packages and from shifting costs onto sicker enrollees in the regulated market.

outcome.mechanism: Supporters couldn't get the 60 votes needed to end debate and hold a final vote — it failed 55-43, almost entirely along party lines — so the bill never came up for an up-or-down vote and died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate HELP Committee, chaired by the bill's sponsor, reported it favorably with a substitute amendment on April 27, 2006, and it was placed on the Senate calendar [S6].
On May 9, 2006, the Senate voted 96-2 to cut off debate on the motion to proceed, with 42 of 44 Democrats and 53 of 55 Republicans in favor [S7].
On May 11, 2006, cloture on the modified committee substitute failed 55-43, short of the 60 needed; Democrats voted 2-41 against ending debate while Republicans voted 53-1 for it [S8].
The bill was returned to the Senate calendar on July 27, 2006, and received no further action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State insurance regulators and consumers kept their existing state coverage, pricing, and appeal protections. The bill's backers — its Senate sponsors, the associations and insurers it would have benefited — got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators and consumers kept protections

for.name: Sen. Michael Enzi
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, reported it out of committee with a substitute amendment, and managed it on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Bill Frist
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor, moved to recommit it with further amendments, and pressed for a final vote.

for.name: 53 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted to end debate and proceed to a final vote on the modified bill (roll call 119).

for.name: 7 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Ben Nelson of Nebraska as the lone Democrat.

for.name: Small business and trade association groups (including NFIB and chambers of commerce)
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed association health plan legislation as a way for small employers to buy cheaper group coverage.

against.name: 41 of 44 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against ending debate on the modified substitute (roll call 119), keeping it short of the 60 votes needed for a final vote.

against.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
against.what_they_did: Led Senate Democratic opposition, arguing the bill's preemption of state benefit mandates and rating rules would strip consumer protections.

against.name: State insurance commissioners (NAIC)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's preemption of state authority over licensure, benefits, and premium rating.

against.name: Consumer health organizations
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill on the grounds that it would void state-mandated benefits and patient protections.

sides.party_line_note: The vote to open debate was 96-2 with both parties on board, but the decisive vote to end debate on the final version split almost perfectly by party: 53 of 55 Republicans for, 41 of 44 Democrats against.

industries.note: The bill would have let insurers sell plans in any non-adopting state free of that state's benefit mandates, rating limits, and patient protections, and would have given them a federal right to sue states for damages with attorney's fees. The gain comes from weaker regulation of a product sold to ordinary people, not from a cheaper public alternative.

industries.industry: Trade, professional, and business associations (chambers of commerce, franchise networks)
industries.note: Associations would gain a new business line as sponsors of federally certified small business health plans, and franchise companies could sponsor plans for their franchisees. Their small-business members might get cheaper coverage, but the plans could pick thinner benefit packages that shift costs onto sicker enrollees.

industries.industry: Small business owners and the self-employed
industries.note: They could join association plans offering group coverage they might not otherwise afford, with contributions barred from varying by health status or industry. The benefit depends on plans remaining solvent and adequately covering members.

Federal preemption would strip their authority over licensure, rating, benefits, and patient protections for participating insurers, leaving only an informational filing and consultation with a plan's single home state.
